newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican labour union threatens general strike.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican labour union threatens general strike.

text.p: South Africa's largest labour movement Cosatu on Thursday threatened to begin mobilising its members for a general strike over a planned employment bill.
Cosatu has been in an uneasy alliance with the ruling African National Congress of President Nelson Mandela, but any mass action would be the most serious breach between the partners.
"We are mobilising our members because of the deadlock reached in terms of negotiations on the Employment Bill," a Cosatu spokeswoman told Reuters.
Cosatu has a total of 1,9 million members and plans a general strike on May 12.
Since it came to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994 Mandela's government has confounded many of its right-wing critics by pursuing market-friendly policies.

But while the government's commitment to a free market and privatisation has wooed foreign investors and South Africa's still predominantly white business community it has provoked argument with Cosatu and the South African Communist Party.

Cosatu said the main bones of contention with the new law were a government-proposed 45-hour week, while it wants a 40-hour maximum, and the length of paid maternity leave. There Cosatu wants a six-month period, while the government is offering four months.
"We believe that we can't work by the (negotiating) table only. In some cases we will have to show our stength as a labour movement," the Cosatu spokeswoman said.
But Cosatu added that it was still open to talks on the proposed bill -- the terms of which have not yet been put to South Africa's cabinet.

Cosatu's move to prepare for a strike came as a shock to the Minister of Labour, Tito Mboweni. "I am extremely surprised to hear that Cosatu is due to begin a process to mobilise its membership towards a possible general strike," he said in a statement.

Mboweni said the terms of the planned legislation were still open to discussion. "The cabinet has not finalised its position on the employment bill and will be doing so in the next couple of weeks, once the bill is formally submitted to it," he added.

The news of a serious labour dispute may dishearten foreign investors who have recently been flooding into the country on the back of a buoyant rand that has started to claw back some of the ground it lost last year.
Earlier on Monday Finance Minister Trevor Manuel gave the bullish markets a fresh lease of life by announcing that the government would meet its budget deficit target in the year to end-March.
